doc_summary: METR paper proposing the 50%-task-completion time horizon metric, measured on HCAST, RE-Bench and new SWAA tasks against human baselines, showing ~7-month doubling. It repeatedly interrogates how far its benchmark tasks differ from real work (messiness, context, scoring) and what that means for external validity.

items.claim: Prefers real, economically valuable, uncontaminated work (e.g. internal PRs scored manually like real reviews) over artificial auto-scorable benchmark tasks because benchmark tasks may not generalize to real-world performance.
items.quote: Resolving these issues was real work performed by internal staff, so we might expect results on these tasks to better represent performance on real economically valuable tasks than a typical benchmark task.

items.claim: In a setup, include the properties of real tasks (dynamic environments, other agents, resource limits, punishing mistakes, no automatic scorer) instead of static, forgiving, cleanly scored environments because those differences are what make benchmark tasks systematically unlike real work.
items.quote: realistic tasks rarely have automatic scoring, and often require dealing with other agents, resource constraints, dynamic environments, and high reliability requirements. Such differences cast doubt on whether the rapid performance improvements seen on this task suite (and other benchmarks) will generalize.

items.claim: In a setup, leave out explicit hints, clean file names and verification mechanisms, making the task under-specified and messy, instead of handing the agent tidy signposts, because messy details are what distinguish real work from benchmarks.
items.quote: Real-world intellectual labor often involves messy details that benchmarks usually don't include, such as being under-specified or poorly scoped, having unclear feedback loops or success criteria, or requiring coordination between multiple streams of work in real-time.

items.claim: Expects that features making a task harder or more artificial for humans can change model behavior in unexpected ways, so manipulations of task surface features should be tested rather than assumed.
items.quote: factors that make humans worse at some tasks may indeed improve agent performance.

items.claim: Prefers realism that is built by simplification-free, real-life-sourced tasks over intentionally simplified subtasks, because simplification into isolated units strips the context real work has.
items.quote: Is this task: EITHER 1. Intended to be representative of some real world end-to-end task (if uncertain, is more likely than not) OR 2. Sourced from a real-life problem AND 3. Has NOT been intentionally simplified to an easier and smaller subtask.

items.claim: Distrusts benchmarks adversarially filtered against current models and benchmarks that saturate, because selection effects bias the comparison and limit meaning.
items.quote: benchmarks are often adversarially selected for tasks that current models struggle with compared to humans, biasing the comparison to human performance.

items.claim: Blinds task authors to model performance and uses a held-out dev set for elicitation, to avoid overfitting tasks or scaffolds to the models being measured.
items.quote: Development of SWAA tasks was blind to AI agent performance; that is, all tasks were written before seeing AI attempts, and elicitation (development of the few-shot prompt used for evaluation) was carried out on a separate development task suite.

items.claim: Accepts a headline result only after checking it across external-validity probes (alternate benchmark, messiness split, real PRs) and sensitivity analyses, rather than trusting a single measurement, and is more confident in slopes than in point estimates.
items.quote: While there are wide error bars on each individual models' horizon lengths, these errors are highly correlated between models. [...] Therefore, we are more confident in the slope of the time horizon trend than in the time horizon of any particular model.

items.claim: Distrusts evidence from their own analysis choices when those choices were selected for being relevant to model failure, flagging selection bias in the messiness factors.
items.quote: A limitation of our messiness factors is that they are at least somewhat adversarially selected against current models.

items.claim: Reads transcripts qualitatively (random samples of failed runs, categorized) to explain quantitative trends rather than relying on aggregate scores alone.
items.quote: By examining transcripts from 31 randomly sampled unsuccessful GPT-4 1106 agent runs and 32 o1 runs, we observe that models seem to have improved greatly in terms of tool use capabilities

items.claim: Calls for more natural, varied tasks involving other agents, humans, mouse interaction and high reliability requirements, and other domains.
items.quote: No tasks require cooperating or competing with humans or other agents, while real software engineering or ML research involves communicating and coordinating with managers and other engineers or researchers.
